title: Words and Pictures
subtitle: A girl grows up in Tehran and draws her country in black ink. How does a comic tell a story that words alone cannot?

card.essence: A memoir drawn in stark black and white. How to read a panel — the words, the picture and the gap between them — and why the simplest drawings can carry the heaviest subjects.

intention: you'll learn how a graphic memoir makes meaning through words, pictures and the gaps between panels, and use a four-step method to write and talk about any page, so you can analyse images with the same precision as sentences.
warmup: Has a picture or a photograph ever told you more than a paragraph of words? What did it show?
What can a drawing do that a written description cannot — and what can writing do that a drawing cannot?
If you wanted to explain a painful memory to a stranger, would you choose words, pictures or both? Why?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: On this page of the comic there are six panels, each one a small box that shows a single moment.
items.meaning: panel — one framed picture in a comic. A page is built from a sequence of panels.

items.sent: Readers must imagine what happens in the white gutter between two panels, because nothing is drawn there.
items.meaning: gutter — the blank space between panels, where the reader supplies what is missing.

items.sent: The caption at the top of the panel tells us the year, while the picture shows a street full of people.
items.meaning: caption — a short piece of text in a box, usually the narrator's voice, separate from a speech bubble.

items.sent: The juxtaposition of a child's toy and a burned building in one image makes the viewer uncomfortable.
items.meaning: juxtaposition — placing two very different things side by side so that the contrast creates meaning.

vocab.heading: B · Describing the style
vocab.intro: Same method: guess from the sentence, then reveal.

items.sent: The drawing is stark: only black ink and white paper, with no grey and no decoration.
items.meaning: stark (adjective) — plain, severe and without softening; harshly simple.

items.sent: The faces are stylised: a few lines for the eyes and mouth, rather than a realistic portrait.
items.meaning: stylised (adjective) — drawn in a simplified, deliberate style rather than as an exact copy of reality.

items.sent: A single image can convey fear without using a word, simply through the size and position of a figure.
items.meaning: convey (verb) — to communicate an idea, feeling or message.

vocab.heading: C · Talking about effects
vocab.intro: Three words you will need to explain what a page does. Guess, then reveal.

items.sent: The tone of the caption is calm and factual, even though the event it describes is frightening.
items.meaning: tone (noun) — the attitude or feeling in the way something is expressed: calm, bitter, playful, cold.

items.sent: In many stories, a locked door can symbolise a lack of freedom without anyone mentioning it.
items.meaning: symbolise (verb) — to stand for an idea: a simple object that represents something bigger.

items.sent: The ending of the page has a certain ambiguity: the smile could mean relief or it could mean fear.
items.meaning: ambiguity (noun) — a quality of having more than one possible meaning, so the reader must decide.

vocab_use: Describe a poster or an image you remember where the tone and the subject did not match.
What object could symbolise freedom, and what could symbolise its loss? Explain your choice.
Describe a moment in a film where a gap — something left out — made you feel more than if it had been shown.
story_heading: How a comic about a country was made

story.heading: Part 1 — A memoir that began in France
paras: Marjane Satrapi was born in 1969 and grew up in Tehran, the capital of Iran. As a young adult she left the country, and she later lived in Paris. Between 2000 and 2003 she published her life story in French as a comic, in four volumes, under the title Persepolis — the Greek name for the ancient Persian capital.

It is a memoir: a true account of her own childhood and youth. It begins when she is a child of about ten, in the years when Iran's government fell and a new, much stricter one took its place, and it follows her through war, through teenage years abroad in Europe and back to Tehran.

English readers met it a few years later, and it became one of the best-known graphic memoirs in the world. In 2007 Satrapi and a co-director turned it into an animated film, which shared a Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival and was nominated for an Oscar for Best Animated Feature.
checks: In which language did Persepolis first appear, and over what years?
What does it mean to call the book a memoir?
answers: In French, in four volumes, between 2000 and 2003.
It is a true account of the author's own life, told by herself.
It was made into an animated film, which shared a Jury Prize at Cannes and was nominated for an Oscar.
story.discuss: Why might someone choose to tell a true story about their country in a comic, not an essay or a novel?

story.heading: Part 2 — How a page of comics works
paras: A comic page is built from panels: small boxes, each showing one moment. Words appear in two main ways — in captions, which usually carry the narrator's voice, and in speech bubbles, which carry what characters say. The picture and the words never do exactly the same job.

Between the panels is the gutter, the white space where nothing is drawn. The comics scholar Scott McCloud argued in his book Understanding Comics that readers fill this gap themselves: we see a person raise a fist in one panel and a broken window in the next, and our mind joins them into an event that is not drawn. McCloud called this closure.

So a comic asks more of its reader than it seems to. Part of the story is on the page, and part is made in the reader's head. The author controls what to show, what to hide and how long we spend looking.
checks: What are the two main ways words appear in a comic?
What does the reader do in the gap between panels?
answers: In captions (the narrator's voice) and in speech bubbles (what characters say).
The blank space between panels.
The reader supplies what is missing and joins two moments into one event.
story.discuss: Think of a film cut that works like the gutter: two shots, and the audience fills in what happens between them.

story.heading: Part 3 — Why black and white?
paras: Satrapi's drawings are stark. They use only black ink on white paper, with bold shapes and simple, stylised faces. There are no shadows, no grey and almost no background detail. A page can look childlike at first, as if a child had drawn it.

That simplicity does real work. Critics have suggested that a plain style lets readers in different countries see themselves in the characters rather than treating them as exotic strangers. It also creates a strong juxtaposition: a child's simple drawing style set against the very adult events of revolution, war and loss.

Imagine a panel, drawn in this style, where a small figure sits calmly at a table while the caption describes something frightening in an even tone. The calm voice and the frightening fact pull against each other, and the reader feels the tension without being told to. That is how a stark style can convey more than a detailed one.
checks: Describe Satrapi's drawing style in two or three words.
Why do critics think the simple style helps readers?
What does the imagined panel show about how words and image can interact?
answers: Stark, black and white, simple and stylised.
It lets readers from different places see themselves in the characters instead of seeing exotic strangers.
A calm picture or tone set against a frightening caption creates tension that the reader feels for themselves.
story.discuss: Is a simple drawing style more honest or less honest about a painful subject? Argue one side.

tool_tab.lead: Reading a comic well means reading three layers at once — then saying what they do together. The Panel Cycle gives you four steps that work on any page, from any comic, film still or painting.
how: Words. Read the caption and any speech first. Note the tone: calm, bitter, playful, formal. Write one phrase, not a summary.
Image. Look at what is drawn: size, position, expression, what is shown large and what is small. Describe it as a camera would — before you interpret.
Gap. Ask what the page does not say or show. What do we have to imagine or connect? Is anything left out on purpose?
Effect. Join the three: what does the combination make the reader feel or understand, and how? Say it in one sentence: By setting … against …, the page makes the reader …

sort.intro: These are observations about an imagined page. Which step of the cycle is each one?

items.text: The caption says the family is “perfectly calm”.
items.why: it reports what is written, in the narrator's own phrase.

items.text: The mother's hands are drawn gripping the edge of the table.
items.why: it describes what is drawn, as a camera would.

items.text: We understand that the calm is pretended, although nobody says so.
items.why: it is something we infer, not written and not drawn.

items.text: The contrast makes the reader uneasy and a little protective of the family.
items.why: it states what the combination does to the reader.

items.text: A tall black figure fills the panel while the child sits tiny in one corner.
items.why: size and position are visual facts.

items.text: The caption does not mention fear at all.
items.why: it is about what is written — and what the written text omits.

items.text: The reader has to connect two panels to see that time has passed.
items.why: the connection happens in the space between panels.

items.text: The plain drawing makes the scene feel both childlike and sinister.
items.why: it names the overall impression the page creates.

breaks: It can become a checklist. Four steps are a way in, not a formula. The best analysis shows how the steps work together; do not list them one by one.
Not every page has a gap. Sometimes the words and the picture simply agree. Then say so, and ask why the author wanted agreement here.
Effect is a claim, not a fact. Two readers can feel different things. Support your effect with the exact word or detail that caused it.
discuss: Which of the four steps do you tend to skip — and what do you miss when you skip it?
Try the cycle on a film still or an advert you know well. Which step is hardest to do?

grammar.name: Writing about a text in the present
grammar.lead: When you write about a book, a comic or a film, you describe it in the present tense — even if the events in the story happened long ago. The history around the text, and the author's life, go in the past.
notes: 1 · The literary present. Describe what happens in the text in the present simple: “The caption describes the calm; the picture shows a tense mother.” Not described or showed.
2 · The author's choices. Use the present for what the author does on the page: “Satrapi uses black ink to…”, “She leaves the gutter empty so that…”.
3 · History and biography. Use the past for events outside the text: “Satrapi published the first volume in 2000.” “The government changed in 1979.”
4 · Events before the moment you describe. Use the present perfect or the past for what has happened earlier in the story: “By this page, the family has already lost a friend.”
5 · Do not mix tenses in one sentence without a reason. The narrator describes the street and then she walked home. → “…and then walks home.”

exercises.heading: Choose the correct tense
exercises.intro: Write the verb in brackets in the correct form. Decide: is it the text, the author's choice, or history?
items: 1. On the first page, the narrator ___ (wear) a veil to school.
2. The author ___ (publish) the first volume in 2000.
3. The caption ___ (contrast) with the image beside it.
4. In 1979 the government of the country ___ (fall).
5. Through the empty gutter, the reader ___ (join) two moments into one event.
answers: 1. wears (the text, present)
2. published (history of the book, past)
3. contrasts (the text, present)
4. fell (history, past)
5. joins (how the text works, present)

exercises.heading: Fix the tense
exercises.intro: Each sentence has one tense mistake for writing about a text. Rewrite the sentence.
items: 1. The narrator described her school and then she showed us the classroom.
2. Satrapi uses black ink and she publishes the book in French in 2000.
3. At the end of the first volume, the child was sent abroad.
4. The image shows a girl who stood alone in the playground.
5. The caption is calm and the picture was tense.
answers: 1. The narrator describes her school and then shows us the classroom.
2. Satrapi uses black ink and published the book in French in 2000.
3. At the end of the first volume, the child is sent abroad.
4. The image shows a girl who stands alone in the playground.
5. The caption is calm and the picture is tense.

exercises.heading: Rewrite as analysis
exercises.intro: Rewrite each plot summary in the correct tense for writing about a text.
items: 1. The girl looked at the soldiers and she felt afraid. → ___
2. The artist chose black ink, and the pages looked stark. → ___
3. Two panels showed a fist and a window; the reader imagined the rest. → ___
answers: 1. The girl looks at the soldiers and feels afraid.
2. The artist chooses black ink, and the pages look stark.
3. Two panels show a fist and a window; the reader imagines the rest.

grammar.closing: Now say three sentences about a film or a book you know, using the present tense for the story and the past for its history.

speak.intro: Now use the cycle and the present tense on your own material. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “The caption … while the image …” · “What is left out is …” · “By setting … against …, the page makes the reader …” · “The effect is …” · “This is conveyed through …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — A picture that says more
paras: Describe an image, photograph or drawing that told you more than words could. What did it show, and what did you have to imagine?

tasks.label: Task 2 — Run the cycle
paras: Choose a still from any film, comic or advert you know. Take us through Words, Image, Gap and Effect, in order.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Taken seriously
paras: A friend thinks comics are only for children. Explain why a graphic memoir deserves to be taken seriously.

tasks.label: Task 4 — Honest in pictures?
paras: Is it easier to be honest in words or in pictures? Argue one side, then give the best point for the other.

final: Satrapi chose the simplest possible drawing for some of the hardest subjects. When is simplicity stronger than detail?
A comic leaves gaps and trusts the reader to fill them. What does that say about how an author sees their audience?
Can a drawing be evidence of what happened? How is it different from a photograph?
From memory: name the four steps of the Panel Cycle and say what each one looks for.
